warmup.q: open class Base { fun grams(g: Int): Base = this } and class GiftBox : Base() { fun ribbon(c: String): GiftBox = this }. Which chain compiles?
options: Both, because the object is a GiftBox either way
warmup.why: Each call returns its declared type. ribbon returns a GiftBox, so grams can follow. grams returns a Base, and Base has no ribbon, even though the object really is a GiftBox. The compiler goes by static types, which is the problem self types solve.

opening:
Orders at the fruit shop come on printed forms. Every form starts with the same lines: the variety, the weight, a note. A gift-box form adds a line for the ribbon, and a delivery form adds a line for the address. A helper fills it in one line at a time.

Here is the odd part. The helper fills in the weight on a gift-box form, and what comes back is "an order form". The ribbon line is still printed on the paper, but nobody is allowed to look at it any more.

In code, the form is a builder, and the trap sits in its base class. A shared setter can only promise to return the base class, so a chain of calls loses the subclass halfway along.

KClass, Class and type tokens ended on that question. In this lesson, we'll give the base form a blank that each kind of form fills with its own name, take null out of a type with T & Any, see how List<out E> can take an E in contains, and finish with function types, Nothing and type aliases. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started at the counter, where a gift-box form came back as "an order form". A recursive bound puts a blank at the top of the base form, and each subclass writes its own name there, so every shared setter hands back the right kind of form. T & Any says a box holds a real fruit, @UnsafeVariance lets the display case answer without opening, and Nothing fits every label.

Now search your code for return this as in a base class, or @UnsafeVariance on a parameter that gets stored. Each one is a promise nobody checks.

Next, we'll build four small designs that use the whole track. How do you store a listener for apples among listeners for any fruit?

sections.h: A form that names itself: a recursive bound keeps the builder chain typed
sections.html:
A builder is an object you fill in one setting at a time and then ask to build the finished thing. Each setter returns the builder, so the calls can follow each other on one line, a style called a fluent chain. Put the shared setters in a base class, add a subclass with a setter of its own, and the chain breaks as soon as a base setter runs:

Java
class PlainBuilder {
    protected int grams;
    PlainBuilder grams(int grams) { this.grams = grams; return this; }
}
class PlainGiftBoxBuilder extends PlainBuilder {
    PlainGiftBoxBuilder ribbon(String colour) { ... }
}

new PlainGiftBoxBuilder().grams(1_200).ribbon("red");   // error: cannot find symbol
Kotlin
open class PlainBuilder {
    protected var grams = 0
    fun grams(grams: Int): PlainBuilder { this.grams = grams; return this }
}
class PlainGiftBoxBuilder : PlainBuilder() {
    fun ribbon(colour: String): PlainGiftBoxBuilder { ... }
}

PlainGiftBoxBuilder().grams(1_200).ribbon("red")
// error: Unresolved reference 'ribbon' on receiver of type 'PlainBuilder'.

grams returns a PlainBuilder, because that's all the base class knows about itself. The object is still a PlainGiftBoxBuilder, and the demo prints that run-time class. But the static type, the one the compiler goes by, has lost it. The form has forgotten what kind of form it is.

The base class needs a way to say "I return whatever subclass I really am". The answer is a self type, a type parameter that stands for "my own subclass", written with a recursive bound, a bound that mentions the type parameter itself:

Java
abstract class Builder<B extends Builder<B>> {
    protected int grams;
    B grams(int grams) { this.grams = grams; return self(); }
    protected abstract B self();
}
final class GiftBoxBuilder extends Builder<GiftBoxBuilder> {
    GiftBoxBuilder ribbon(String colour) { ...; return this; }
    @Override protected GiftBoxBuilder self() { return this; }
}
Kotlin
abstract class Builder<B : Builder<B>> {
    protected var grams = 0
    fun grams(grams: Int): B { this.grams = grams; return self() }
    protected abstract fun self(): B
}
class GiftBoxBuilder : Builder<GiftBoxBuilder>() {
    fun ribbon(colour: String): GiftBoxBuilder { ...; return this }
    override fun self() = this
}

Read B : Builder<B> as "B is a builder whose own B is B". It's the blank at the top of the base form: "this is a ___ form". The only types that fit are subclasses that write their own name in it, as GiftBoxBuilder : Builder<GiftBoxBuilder>() does. Then substitute, as in lesson 1 of this track: for a GiftBoxBuilder, every B in the base class reads as GiftBoxBuilder. So GiftBoxBuilder().grams(1_200) has the static type GiftBoxBuilder, and .ribbon("red") is in reach again. You've met the shape before. Lesson 2's T : Comparable<T>, "a T that compares with its own kind", is a recursive bound, and so is Java's own Enum<E extends Enum<E>>.

Two details matter. The abstract self() keeps the code checked: each subclass returns this, and the compiler verifies that it is a B. The tempting shortcut, return this as B in the base class, is an unchecked cast, and erasure turns it into no check at all. And the bound can't force honesty. class Liar : Builder<GiftBoxBuilder>() compiles, because the blank only asks for the name of some builder. Here the form picture breaks just as the code does: anyone can write another form's name in the blank. With an abstract self(), the liar must hand back a GiftBoxBuilder it doesn't have, which is where you notice.

A recursive bound lets a base class return its subclass. Fill the blank with the subclass's own name.

In pure Kotlin code you often don't need a builder at all: a data class with default arguments and copy covers most cases. Reach for self types when Java callers need a builder, or when you extend a Java class that already uses one. Next, a smaller tool with a big promise: this box is never empty.

The subclass declaration, class GiftBoxBuilder extends Builder of GiftBoxBuilder, writes the subclass's own name into the blank B."><text class="t-s t-m" x="15" y="20">with a self type</text><rect class="box" x="15" y="30" width="190" height="38" rx="8"/><text class="t-s t-code" x="110" y="54" text-anchor="middle">GiftBoxBuilder()</text><line class="ln-a" x1="207" y1="49" x2="243" y2="49" marker-end="url(#arr)"/><rect class="box-a" x="245" y="30" width="210" height="38" rx="8"/><text class="t-s t-code" x="350" y="54" text-anchor="middle">.grams(1_200): B</text><line class="ln-a" x1="457" y1="49" x2="493" y2="49" marker-end="url(#arr)"/><rect class="box-ok" x="495" y="30" width="190" height="38" rx="8"/><text class="t-s t-code" x="590" y="54" text-anchor="middle">.ribbon("red")</text><text class="t-s t-a" x="350" y="88" text-anchor="middle">B = GiftBoxBuilder</text><text class="t-s t-m" x="15" y="126">without one</text><rect class="box" x="15" y="136" width="190" height="38" rx="8"/><text class="t-s t-code" x="110" y="160" text-anchor="middle">PlainGiftBoxBuilder()</text><line class="ln-a" x1="207" y1="155" x2="243" y2="155" marker-end="url(#arr)"/><rect class="box" x="245" y="136" width="210" height="38" rx="8"/><text class="t-s t-code" x="350" y="160" text-anchor="middle">.grams(1_200)</text><line class="ln-a" x1="457" y1="155" x2="493" y2="155" marker-end="url(#arr)"/><rect class="box-bad" x="495" y="136" width="190" height="38" rx="8"/><text class="t-s t-code" x="590" y="160" text-anchor="middle">.ribbon("red")</text><text class="t-s t-m" x="350" y="194" text-anchor="middle">returns PlainBuilder</text><text class="t-s t-bad" x="590" y="194" text-anchor="middle">Unresolved reference</text><rect class="box-dim" x="15" y="214" width="670" height="38" rx="8"/><text class="t-s t-code" x="350" y="238" text-anchor="middle">class GiftBoxBuilder : Builder<GiftBoxBuilder>()    // the subclass writes its own name in B</text></svg>

sections.h: This box always holds a real fruit: T & Any takes null out of a type
sections.html:
A plain T may stand for a nullable type, because its default bound is Any? (lesson 2). On a label, that's "Box of ___", where the caller may write "apples, or nothing". Sometimes you know that one particular value is not null, and you want its type to say so: whatever the label allows, this box holds a real fruit. Kotlin writes that as T & Any, a definitely non-nullable type: "T, with null taken out".

Java
// Java's types say nothing about null. The best you can do is a comment and a check at run time.
static <T> T firstNotNullValue(List<T> items) {
    for (T item : items) if (item != null) return item;
    throw new NoSuchElementException("no non-null element");
}

String first = firstNotNullValue(Arrays.asList(null, "Gala", "Fuji"));
Kotlin
fun <T> List<T>.firstNotNullValue(): T & Any {
    for (item in this) if (item != null) return item     // smart cast: item is T & Any here
    throw NoSuchElementException("no non-null element")
}

val first: String = listOf(null, "Gala", "Fuji").firstNotNullValue()   // T = String?, result String

With T = String?, T & Any is String. With T = Apple, it's just Apple. Inside the loop, the check item != null is what makes item fit: a smart cast, Kotlin's narrowing of a value's type after a check, turns T into T & Any. The compiler holds you to the promise. Return a plain T, and it says Return type mismatch: expected 'T (of fun <T> forget) & Any', actual 'T (of fun <T> forget)'.

The Kotlin docs name the main use: overriding Java methods whose generic parameters are annotated @NotNull, a marker that tells tools a value is never null. Kotlin reads @NotNull T in a Java interface as T & Any:

Java
public interface NotNullTransformer<T> {
    @NotNull T transform(@NotNull T value);
}
Kotlin
class UpperCaser<T : CharSequence?> : NotNullTransformer<T> {
    override fun transform(value: T & Any): T & Any = ...
}

Two rules come with it. The left side must be a type parameter with a nullable bound. With T : Any there is no null to take out, and the compiler says Intersection types are supported only for definitely non-nullable types: left part must be a type parameter with nullable bounds. And the promise is Kotlin's alone: Java sees <T> T firstNotNullValue(List<T>), with no trace of & Any.

The docs add that when you work only with Kotlin, you'll rarely need to write it, because inference handles it. Expect to type T & Any at the Java boundary and in small helpers like this one, which turns an optional field into a value the rest of the code can use without !!, Kotlin's "trust me, it isn't null" operator:

Java
// Java: the null check happens, but the type can't record it
static <T> T requireValue(T value, String name) {
    if (value == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException(name + " is required");
    return value;
}
Kotlin
fun <T> T.requireValue(name: String): T & Any = this ?: throw IllegalArgumentException("$name is required")

val ribbon: String = order.ribbon.requireValue("ribbon")   // order.ribbon is a String?

T & Any is T with null taken out. Use it where a nullable T is known to hold a value.

That was a type with one door closed. Next, a type with one door opened on purpose.

steps: Run NonNullDemo (or NonNullDemoJava). Open NotNullTransformer.java next to it: a Java interface marked with @NotNull.
Uncomment wrong moves 1 and 2 in NonNullDemo.kt one at a time. Predict each error first.
Uncomment function 3 at the bottom. In the Java twin, uncomment the oops line and run: what does Java catch, and when?

code.title: NonNullDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.generics.l10.demo /** T may be nullable (String?), but the result is "T, definitely not null". */ fun <T> List<T>.firstNotNullValue(): T & Any { for (item in this) if (item != null) return item // smart cast: item is T & Any here throw NoSuchElementException("no non-null element") } /** The docs' example: fall back to a value that is known not to be null. */ fun <T> elvis(x: T, y: T & Any): T & Any = x ?: y /** Implements the Java interface in NotNullTransformer.java, whose methods are annotated @NotNull. */ class UpperCaser<T : CharSequence?> : NotNullTransformer<T> { @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST") override fun transform(value: T & Any): T & Any = value.toString().uppercase() as (T & Any) } fun main() { val varieties: List<String?> = listOf(null, "Gala", "Fuji") // the first order form left it blank val first: String = varieties.firstNotNullValue() // T = String?, result String val note: String? = null val shown: String = elvis(note, "no note") println("first = $first, shown = $shown") println("transformed = ${UpperCaser<String?>().transform("Gala")}") // Wrong moves. Uncomment one at a time, predict the error, then run. // fun <T> forget(x: T): T & Any = x // 1 // val n: String = UpperCaser<String?>().transform(null) // 2 } // 3. & Any needs a type parameter whose bound is nullable. // fun <T : Any> pointless(x: T & Any) {}

alt.title: NonNullDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.generics.l10.demo; import java.util.Arrays; import java.util.List; import java.util.NoSuchElementException; import java.util.Objects; /** * Java twin of NonNullDemo.kt. Java types say nothing about null, so "T, but not null" can only be * a convention (or an annotation such as @NotNull), checked at run time. */ public class NonNullDemoJava { static <T> T firstNotNullValue(List<T> items) { for (T item : items) if (item != null) return item; throw new NoSuchElementException("no non-null element"); } static <T> T elvis(T x, T y) { return x != null ? x : Objects.requireNonNull(y); } public static void main(String[] args) { List<String> varieties = Arrays.asList(null, "Gala", "Fuji"); String first = firstNotNullValue(varieties); String shown = elvis(null, "no note"); System.out.println("first = " + first + ", shown = " + shown); System.out.println("transformed = " + new UpperCaser<String>().transform("Gala")); // Uncomment and run: it compiles in Java. What happens at run time? // String oops = elvis(null, null); } }

try.expect: Both print first = Gala, shown = no note and transformed = GALA. Kotlin's wrong moves: (1) Return type mismatch: expected 'T (of fun <T> forget) & Any', actual 'T (of fun <T> forget)'., (2) Null cannot be a value of a non-null type 'String'., because for T = String?, T & Any is String. Function 3: Intersection types are supported only for definitely non-nullable types: left part must be a type parameter with nullable bounds. The Java oops line compiles, and throws NullPointerException from Objects.requireNonNull when it runs.

sections.h: A display case you can ask but not fill: @UnsafeVariance and List.contains
sections.html:
Here's a puzzle left over from lesson 4. List is declared interface List<out E>: it's the glass display case of lesson 3, where things come out and nothing goes in. An out type parameter can't appear as a parameter. Yet you call list.contains(x) every day, and hand it an E. The standard library's source (2.4.21) shows how:

public operator fun contains(element: @UnsafeVariance E): Boolean
public fun indexOf(element: @UnsafeVariance E): Int

@UnsafeVariance "suppresses errors about variance conflict" for one use of the type. Think of it as a note the author tapes to the glass: "this opening is only for pointing". contains compares the element with what's inside and never keeps it. So a List<Int> seen as a List<Number> can't be damaged by it, and contains(2.5) just returns false. The clerk reads the note, nods, and stops checking that one spot.

Why take an E at all, when Any? would need no annotation? Because the E lets the compiler catch a question that makes no sense. Java chose Object, and pays for it:

Java
Set<Long> crateIds = Set.of(42L);
crateIds.contains(42);                        // false: 42 is boxed to an Integer, and Integer(42) != Long(42)
List.of(180, 150).contains("180");            // compiles, always false
Kotlin
val crateIds: Set<Long> = setOf(42L)
crateIds.contains(42)                         // true: the literal 42 is typed as a Long here
listOf(180, 150).contains("180")
// error: Type inference failed. The value of the type parameter 'T' must be mentioned in input types ...

That first Java line is a real kind of bug: an int id looked up in a set of Longs, false every time, with no warning.

The annotation is called unsafe for a reason. It switches the check off, and the compiler believes you. Here is a display case with a secret slot cut into the glass:

Java
// Java's way to break a ? extends view on purpose is an unchecked cast:
List<Apple> apples = new ArrayList<>(List.of(new Apple("Gala", 180)));
List<? extends Fruit> view = apples;
((List<Fruit>) view).add(new Lemon("Eureka", 120));
Apple last = apples.get(apples.size() - 1);     // ClassCastException
Kotlin
class DisplayCase<out T>(first: T) {
    private val items = mutableListOf(first)
    fun add(item: @UnsafeVariance T) { items.add(item) }   // keeps it: a broken promise
    fun last(): T = items.last()
}

val apples: DisplayCase<Apple> = DisplayCase(Apple("Gala", 180))
val anyFruit: DisplayCase<Fruit> = apples       // fine: DisplayCase is out T
anyFruit.add(Lemon("Eureka", 120))              // compiles
val last: Apple = apples.last()                 // ClassCastException

It's lesson 3's lemon in the crate of apples, back again. The demo prints ClassCastException: class workbench.generics.l10.demo.Lemon cannot be cast to class workbench.generics.l10.demo.Apple.

Use @UnsafeVariance only on parameters that are read and compared, such as those of contains, indexOf or an equality check, never on ones that are kept. To check that a use is honest, follow the parameter through the body. If it only reaches ==, equals or hashCode, the promise holds. If it reaches a field, a collection or a callback that keeps it, remove the annotation and make the type invariant, or split it into a read view and a write view, as lesson 11 of this track does.

@UnsafeVariance is a promise, not a check. Put it only on parameters that are compared, never kept.

Three more tools sit at the edges of the type system, and one of them is a box that can never hold anything.

steps: Run UnsafeVarianceDemo and UnsafeVarianceDemoJava. Find the line that compiles in Java and is refused in Kotlin.
Uncomment wrong move 1 in the Kotlin file. Predict, then run.
Uncomment wrong move 2 (DisplayCase2) and read the error. That's the check @UnsafeVariance switched off in DisplayCase.

code.title: UnsafeVarianceDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.generics.l10.demo // The shop's fruit, used by the demos of this lesson (the Java twins use these Kotlin types too) interface Fruit { val name: String; val grams: Int } data class Apple(override val name: String, override val grams: Int) : Fruit { override fun toString() = name } data class Lemon(override val name: String, override val grams: Int) : Fruit { override fun toString() = name } /** Declared out, like a glass display case. Then someone cut a slot in the glass for add(). It compiles. */ class DisplayCase<out T>(first: T) { private val items = mutableListOf(first) fun add(item: @UnsafeVariance T) { items.add(item) } fun last(): T = items.last() } fun main() { // 1. The standard library uses @UnsafeVariance safely: contains only compares, it never stores. val weights: List<Number> = listOf(180, 150) // List<Int> seen as List<Number> println("contains(150): ${weights.contains(150)}, contains(2.5): ${weights.contains(2.5)}") // 2. And because contains takes an E, the compiler can catch a nonsense check. // println(listOf(180, 150).contains("180")) // wrong move 1 // 3. Used carelessly, the same annotation breaks type safety. val apples: DisplayCase<Apple> = DisplayCase(Apple("Gala", 180)) val anyFruit: DisplayCase<Fruit> = apples // fine: DisplayCase is out T anyFruit.add(Lemon("Eureka", 120)) // compiles, thanks to @UnsafeVariance try { val last: Apple = apples.last() println(last) } catch (e: ClassCastException) { println("ClassCastException: ${e.message?.substringBefore(" (")}") } } // Wrong move 2: remove @UnsafeVariance from a copy of DisplayCase and read the error. // class DisplayCase2<out T> { fun add(item: T) {} }

alt.title: UnsafeVarianceDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.generics.l10.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** * Java twin of UnsafeVarianceDemo.kt. Java's contains takes an Object, so it never needed the * annotation, and it can't catch a nonsense check. Java's way to break a ? extends view on purpose * is an unchecked cast. */ public class UnsafeVarianceDemoJava { @SuppressWarnings("unchecked") public static void main(String[] args) { List<? extends Number> weights = List.of(180, 150); System.out.println("contains(150): " + weights.contains(150) + ", contains(2.5): " + weights.contains(2.5)); System.out.println("contains(\"180\") compiles in Java: " + List.of(180, 150).contains("180")); List<Apple> apples = new ArrayList<>(List.of(new Apple("Gala", 180))); List<? extends Fruit> view = apples; ((List<Fruit>) view).add(new Lemon("Eureka", 120)); // the unchecked cast is the Java "unsafe variance" try { Apple last = apples.get(apples.size() - 1); System.out.println(last); } catch (ClassCastException e) { System.out.println("ClassCastException: " + e.getMessage().split(" \\(")[0]); } } }

Java also prints contains("180") compiles in Java: false. In Kotlin, wrong move 1 fails with Type inference failed. The value of the type parameter 'T' must be mentioned in input types ..., and DisplayCase2 fails with Type parameter 'T' is declared as 'out' but occurs in 'in' position in type 'T (of class DisplayCase2<out T>)'.

sections.h: Three more tools at the edges: function types, Nothing and type aliases
sections.html:
Function types carry variance on both ends. (P) -> R is Function1<in P, out R> (lesson 5): a function takes its parameter in and hands its result out. So a helper that joins two steps accepts a more general second step, and its result can be used as something more general:

Java
// Function<T, R> is invariant, so the JDK writes the variance into the signature:
// default <V> Function<T, V> andThen(Function<? super R, ? extends V> after)
Function<String, Long> toGrams = s -> new BigDecimal(s).movePointRight(3).longValueExact();   // kilograms to grams
Function<Object, String> describe = x -> "<" + x + ">";
Function<String, String> pipeline = toGrams.andThen(describe);      // <1250> for "1.25"
Kotlin
fun <A, B, C> andThen(first: (A) -> B, second: (B) -> C): (A) -> C = { a -> second(first(a)) }

val toGrams: (String) -> Long = { BigDecimal(it).movePointRight(3).longValueExact() }   // kilograms to grams
val describe: (Any) -> String = { "<$it>" }                  // takes Any, not just Long
val pipeline: (String) -> CharSequence = andThen(toGrams, describe)   // <1250> for "1.25"

Nothing is the bottom type: a subtype of every type, with no values at all. It's the one box that can never hold anything, so it fits every label. throw and TODO() have the type Nothing, which is why val strict: Long = text.toLongOrNull() ?: fail("not a number") type-checks when fun fail(reason: String): Nothing. It also explains emptyList(). One shared, empty List<Nothing> fits every List<Apple>, because List is out E and Nothing sits below Apple: an empty display case is a fine apple display. Lesson 11 uses the same trick for Either. Java has no bottom type. Collections.emptyList() is a generic method whose T is inferred at each call, and a Kotlin List<Nothing> reaches Java as a raw List.

A type alias gives an existing type a shorter name, and it can be generic:

Java
// Java has no type aliases. The nearest thing, a functional interface, is a new, separate type.
@FunctionalInterface interface Listener<E> { void hear(E item); }
Kotlin
typealias Listener<E> = (E) -> Unit          // just a name: a Listener<E> IS an (E) -> Unit
typealias Index<K> = MutableMap<K, MutableList<K>>

val signWriter: Listener<Apple> = { println("sign for ${it.name}") }
val plain: (Apple) -> Unit = signWriter      // same type, no conversion

An alias is a nickname written on the label, not a new kind of box. So it has the variance of what it stands for: a Listener<Fruit> is a Listener<Apple>, exactly as with the function type. That's how lesson 5's delivery bell took a stock-keeper who counts every fruit. Aliases nested inside a class became Stable in Kotlin 2.3, with one limit: they can't mention the outer class's type parameters.

All the tools in this lesson share one limit, and it's worth saying plainly: each is a promise the compiler partly takes on trust. A recursive bound can't stop a liar, T & Any means nothing to Java, and @UnsafeVariance is believed without a second look. The lab puts the first and the last of them to work on the shop's order forms.

try.title: Compose with variance, fail with Nothing
steps: Run FunctionTypesDemo (or FunctionTypesDemoJava, which also calls the JDK's own andThen).
Uncomment the wrong move and read which type the compiler found for the pipeline.
Change fail's return type from Nothing to Unit. Which line breaks, and why?

code.title: FunctionTypesDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.generics.l10.demo import java.math.BigDecimal /** A new name for a function type. Not a new type: a Listener<E> IS an (E) -> Unit. */ typealias Listener<E> = (E) -> Unit fun <A, B, C> andThen(first: (A) -> B, second: (B) -> C): (A) -> C = { a -> second(first(a)) } fun fail(reason: String): Nothing = throw IllegalArgumentException(reason) fun main() { // 1. Function1<in P, out R>: a more general second function fits. val toGrams: (String) -> Long = { BigDecimal(it).movePointRight(3).longValueExact() } // kilograms to grams val describe: (Any) -> String = { "<$it>" } val pipeline: (String) -> CharSequence = andThen(toGrams, describe) println("pipeline(\"1.25\") = ${pipeline("1.25")}") // 2. Nothing is a subtype of every type. val none: List<Apple> = emptyList() // emptyList() is a List<Nothing> here val grams: Long = "x".toLongOrNull() ?: 0L val strict: Long = "180".toLongOrNull() ?: fail("not a number") // fail returns Nothing, so this is a Long println("none = $none, grams = $grams, strict = $strict") // 3. A type alias is only a name. val signWriter: Listener<Apple> = { println("sign for ${it.name}") } val plain: (Apple) -> Unit = signWriter // same type, no conversion plain(Apple("Gala", 180)) // Wrong move. Uncomment, predict the error, then run. // val tooStrict: (Any) -> String = andThen(toGrams, describe) }

alt.title: FunctionTypesDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.generics.l10.demo; import java.math.BigDecimal; import java.util.Collections; import java.util.List; import java.util.function.Consumer; import java.util.function.Function; /** * Java twin of FunctionTypesDemo.kt. Java's Function<T, R> is invariant, so the JDK writes the * variance into andThen's signature: andThen(Function<? super R, ? extends V> after). */ public class FunctionTypesDemoJava { static <A, B, C> Function<A, C> andThen(Function<A, ? extends B> first, Function<? super B, ? extends C> second) { return a -> second.apply(first.apply(a)); } static <T> T fail(String reason) { throw new IllegalArgumentException(reason); } // no Nothing: fake it with T public static void main(String[] args) { Function<String, Long> toGrams = s -> new BigDecimal(s).movePointRight(3).longValueExact(); // kilograms to grams Function<Object, String> describe = x -> "<" + x + ">"; Function<String, CharSequence> pipeline = andThen(toGrams, describe); System.out.println("pipeline(\"1.25\") = " + pipeline.apply("1.25")); System.out.println("JDK andThen: " + toGrams.andThen(describe).apply("0.35")); List<Apple> none = Collections.emptyList(); // generic method: T inferred as Apple long strict = Long.parseLong("180"); System.out.println("none = " + none + ", strict = " + strict); Consumer<Apple> signWriter = a -> System.out.println("sign for " + a.getName()); // no type aliases in Java signWriter.accept(new Apple("Gala", 180)); } }

try.expect: Kotlin prints pipeline("1.25") = <1250>, none = [], grams = 0, strict = 180 and sign for Gala. Java prints the pipeline line, JDK andThen: <350>, none = [], strict = 180 and sign for Gala. The wrong move fails with Initializer type mismatch: expected '(Any) -> String', actual '(String) -> String'.: a function that needs a String input can't stand in for one that takes Any. With Unit, the strict line fails with Initializer type mismatch: expected 'Long', actual 'Any'., because the type of the ?: expression becomes the common supertype of Long and Unit. Nothing fits there because it is a subtype of Long.

compare.title: A self-typed order builder in Java and Kotlin

java.title: OrderBuilder.java
java.html: abstract class OrderBuilder<B extends OrderBuilder<B>> { protected int grams; protected String variety; B grams(int grams) { this.grams = grams; return self(); } B variety(String name) { this.variety = name; return self(); } protected abstract B self(); } final class GiftBoxBuilder extends OrderBuilder<GiftBoxBuilder> { private String ribbon; GiftBoxBuilder ribbon(String colour) { this.ribbon = colour; return this; } @Override protected GiftBoxBuilder self() { return this; } GiftBox build() { if (grams <= 0) throw new IllegalStateException("weight must be positive"); return new GiftBox(grams, variety, "", ribbon); } } // new GiftBoxBuilder().grams(1_200).variety("Gala").ribbon("red").build();

kotlin.title: OrderBuilder.kt
kotlin.html: abstract class OrderBuilder<B : OrderBuilder<B>> { protected var grams: Int = 0 protected var variety: String? = null fun grams(grams: Int): B { this.grams = grams; return self() } fun variety(name: String): B { variety = name; return self() } protected abstract fun self(): B } class GiftBoxBuilder : OrderBuilder<GiftBoxBuilder>() { private var ribbon: String? = null fun ribbon(colour: String): GiftBoxBuilder { ribbon = colour; return this } override fun self() = this fun build(): GiftBox { check(grams > 0) { "weight must be positive" } return GiftBox(grams, variety!!, "", checkNotNull(ribbon)) } } // GiftBoxBuilder().grams(1_200).variety("Gala").ribbon("red").build()

compare.note: The recursive bound is the same idea in both languages: B extends OrderBuilder<B> and B : OrderBuilder<B>, with each subclass passing itself and an abstract self() in place of an unchecked cast. Kotlin adds checks Java can't express. variety and ribbon are String?, so build() must deal with a missing value, and check and checkNotNull throw IllegalStateException with your message. Java's build() happily passes a null ribbon along. The other three tools of this lesson have no Java twin: T & Any (Java types carry no nullability), @UnsafeVariance (Java has no declaration-site variance to suppress) and Nothing (Java has no bottom type). Java has no type aliases either. And in Kotlin you can often skip the builder entirely with a data class, default arguments and copy.

worked.title: Add a pickup order to the builder hierarchy

steps.say: The lab's hierarchy has gift boxes and deliveries. The shop wants pickup orders too, collected at the counter at a set time. The quickest path is to copy GiftBoxBuilder and edit it, and that's how the classic bug gets in: the type argument still says GiftBoxBuilder.
steps.code: class PickupBuilder : OrderBuilder<GiftBoxBuilder>() { // copied, not changed private var time: String? = null fun pickupAt(time: String): PickupBuilder { this.time = time; return this } override fun self(): GiftBoxBuilder = this } // error: Return type mismatch: expected 'GiftBoxBuilder', actual 'PickupBuilder'.

alt.html: final class PickupBuilder extends OrderBuilder<GiftBoxBuilder> { // copied, not changed private String time; PickupBuilder pickupAt(String time) { this.time = time; return this; } @Override protected GiftBoxBuilder self() { return this; } } // error: incompatible types: PickupBuilder cannot be converted to GiftBoxBuilder

steps.say: 1. The abstract self() caught it at compile time. With return this as B in the base class, the same slip would compile, and PickupBuilder().grams(500) would throw ClassCastException: class PickupBuilder cannot be cast to class GiftBoxBuilder at the call. Fix the declaration: the subclass writes its own name in the blank.
steps.code: class PickupBuilder : OrderBuilder<PickupBuilder>() { private var time: String? = null fun pickupAt(time: String): PickupBuilder { this.time = time; return this } override fun self() = this // B is PickupBuilder: no cast

alt.html: final class PickupBuilder extends OrderBuilder<PickupBuilder> { private String time; PickupBuilder pickupAt(String time) { this.time = time; return this; } @Override protected PickupBuilder self() { return this; } // no cast

steps.say: 1. Build: check the shared fields with the base class's checkCommon(), then the pickup's own field. Self-check before reading the comment: why does grams(...) in the chain below return a PickupBuilder, with no change to the base class? (Because the declaration fills B with PickupBuilder, and grams returns B.)
steps.code: fun build(): Pickup { checkCommon() val t = checkNotNull(time) { "pickup time is required" } return Pickup(grams, variety!!, note, t) } } val p = PickupBuilder().grams(2_500).variety("Fuji").pickupAt("17:30").build()

alt.html: Pickup build() { checkCommon(); if (time == null) throw new IllegalStateException("pickup time is required"); return new Pickup(grams, variety, note, time); } } Pickup p = new PickupBuilder().grams(2_500).variety("Fuji").pickupAt("17:30").build();

lab.title: A self-typed order builder, and functions with variance
steps: Run the tests. All eight fail. The signatures are done, so read them first, especially OrderBuilder<B : OrderBuilder<B>> and the two subclass declarations.
In Builders.kt, write the three shared setters: store the value, then return self(). Write checkCommon() with two check(...) calls.
Write self(), the setter and build() in GiftBoxBuilder and in DeliveryBuilder. build() calls checkCommon() first, then checks its own field.
In Functions.kt, write andThen as a lambda, and fanOut as a lambda that calls each listener in order. Read the fanOut test: it passes a Listener<Fruit> where a Listener<Apple> is expected.
Write firstNotNullValue with a loop. Notice that returning the smart-cast item satisfies T & Any.
Run the tests until all eight pass.
hints: fun grams(grams: Int): B { this.grams = grams; return self() } is the whole pattern for each shared setter.
checkNotNull(ribbon) { "ribbon is required" } returns the value if it isn't null, or throws IllegalStateException with that message.
andThen is one line: = { a -> second(first(a)) }. fanOut is = { item -> for (l in listeners) l(item) }.

drill.title: Write a self-typed builder from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write an abstract Builder with a recursive bound, one setter grams(n) that returns the subclass type, and an abstract self(). Then write GiftBoxBuilder with ribbon(colour) and build(), so that GiftBoxBuilder().grams(1_200).ribbon("red").build() compiles. Do it in Kotlin, then in Java.

answer.html: abstract class Builder<B : Builder<B>> { protected var grams = 0 fun grams(grams: Int): B { this.grams = grams; return self() } protected abstract fun self(): B } class GiftBoxBuilder : Builder<GiftBoxBuilder>() { // the subclass writes its own name in B private var ribbon = "" fun ribbon(colour: String): GiftBoxBuilder { ribbon = colour; return this } override fun self() = this fun build() = "gift box, $grams g, $ribbon ribbon" }

alt.title: Builder.java
alt.html: abstract class Builder<B extends Builder<B>> { protected int grams; B grams(int grams) { this.grams = grams; return self(); } protected abstract B self(); } final class GiftBoxBuilder extends Builder<GiftBoxBuilder> { // the subclass writes its own name in B private String ribbon = ""; GiftBoxBuilder ribbon(String colour) { ribbon = colour; return this; } @Override protected GiftBoxBuilder self() { return this; } String build() { return "gift box, " + grams + " g, " + ribbon + " ribbon"; } }

recap: A recursive bound, B : Builder<B>, lets a base class name its own subclass, so shared setters can return it and a chain keeps the subclass's methods.
Each subclass writes its own name in the blank (GiftBoxBuilder : Builder<GiftBoxBuilder>()) and implements an abstract self() = this. Avoid this as B: it is unchecked and fails late.
T & Any is "T without null": for T = String? it's String. Its main use is overriding Java generic methods marked @NotNull.
List<out E> declares contains(element: @UnsafeVariance E). That's safe because contains only compares, and the E lets Kotlin refuse listOf(180).contains("180").
Nothing is a subtype of every type, so emptyList() fits any List<T> and ?: fail(...) type-checks. A type alias is only a new name, with the variance of the type it names.
The limit: these tools are partly taken on trust. A subclass can write the wrong name, Java never sees & Any, and @UnsafeVariance on a stored parameter ends in a ClassCastException.

explain.prompt: A teammate sees abstract class OrderBuilder<B : OrderBuilder<B>> in a code review and says it looks circular and pointless. Explain in your own words what problem it solves, how a subclass uses it, and what it can't prevent.
explain.answer: Without it, a setter in the base class can only return the base class type. So after calling grams() on a GiftBoxBuilder, the compiler thinks it has a plain order builder and won't let you call ribbon(). The recursive bound gives the base class a name, B, for "whatever concrete subclass I am", like a blank at the top of a form. Each subclass fills it in with its own name, as in class GiftBoxBuilder : OrderBuilder<GiftBoxBuilder>(), so for that subclass B means GiftBoxBuilder, and every inherited setter returns that type. The bound only looks circular: it reads "B is a builder whose B is B", which only self-naming subclasses satisfy. Each subclass implements self() as this, which the compiler checks, so no unchecked cast is needed. What it can't prevent is a subclass writing the wrong name, such as a pickup builder that says OrderBuilder<GiftBoxBuilder>. The abstract self() turns that slip into a compile error, which is why it's better than this as B.

deeper.html:
Recursive bounds go further than builders. java.lang.Enum is declared Enum<E extends Enum<E>> so that compareTo takes the same enum type, and EnumSet.noneOf(Class<E>) is bounded <E extends Enum<E>>. Kotlin's Enum<E : Enum<E>> is the same declaration. Lesson 2's fun <T : Comparable<T>> maxOf2(a: T, b: T) is the most common recursive bound of all; the Java signature Kotlin generates for it is <T extends Comparable<? super T>>, because Kotlin's Comparable is declared in T.

The standard library's use of @UnsafeVariance is easy to check. In the 2.4.21 sources (kotlin-stdlib-sources.jar, file Collections.kt) it appears on contains, containsAll and indexOf of List, and on AbstractCollection.contains. The contains("180") error you saw comes from a second safety net. When the member contains(element: Int) doesn't accept a String, the compiler tries the extension Iterable<T>.contains(element: T), whose T is marked so that it must match the receiver's element type, and inference fails with the message you read.

Two small facts about Nothing. The type of the literal null is Nothing?, which is why null fits every nullable type. And when a Kotlin function returns List<Nothing>, Java sees a raw List, because Java has no bottom type to write there.

Type aliases can't create the separate types people sometimes want from them. typealias CrateId = String lets you pass any String where a CrateId is expected. If you want the compiler to keep crate ids and supplier ids apart, use a value class, @JvmInline value class CrateId(val value: String), which is a real type with no wrapper object at run time in most uses.
